issues.issue: Dividends are payable only "to the extent, and upon the conditions fixed and determined by the Board of Directors," which makes the promise wholly discretionary and arguably illusory. A court could be asked whether any enforceable entitlement exists at all.

The grant covers "risks of direct physical loss or damage" resulting from "an occurrence," and both "direct physical loss or damage" (does cosmetic or functional impairment count?) and the scope of a single "occurrence" are open to competing readings. This is the core coverage sentence on which any coverage dispute would turn.

The policy is said to consist of the forms on the POLICY INDEX, yet operative conditions cross-refer to Form RM1102 (Schedule of Mortgage Holders or Loss Payees), which is not listed on that index. A court could be asked which documents actually form the contract.
Special meanings are keyed to "bold faced type" and to italics, typographic signals that are unreliable in the issued document; a reader cannot always tell whether a word carries its defined meaning.

The blanket promise of "coverage on a replacement cost basis" sits against VALUATIONS A.2, which withholds replacement cost until property is actually repaired or replaced and reverts to actual cash value after two years. The "except as indicated" proviso may or may not be read to absorb that limitation.

The single-limit-per-"occurrence" cap depends entirely on the DEFINITIONS Z. "Occurrence" clause, which aggregates a "series of similar causes" irrespective of time or area; how many limits apply to repeated storms is left to be argued.
"Coverage may be limited or excluded elsewhere in this policy or its endorsements" states no rule and identifies no provision, leaving the reader unable to tell what it does.

The $10,000 per-occurrence deductible is displaced "unless marked with an X in G.2.", and the X is marked, pointing to Form RM1115, which itself sets deductibles only for named-storm, mobile-equipment and equipment-breakdown categories. Whether the $10,000 still applies to an ordinary wind/hail loss is left unresolved.
The paragraph opens with orphaned sub-letters ("a. d.") and every amount reads "$Not Applicable", so the combined-deductible mechanism cannot be applied as written.

The entry is a sentence fragment beginning "See Form RM1115 times the average daily value", with no multiplier stated in the text itself, so the deductible cannot be computed from this provision alone.
The waiting period is stated as "Not Applicable hours," which is not a number and cannot be applied; it is unclear whether that means no waiting period or no coverage.

The "largest single deductible" rule is subject to exceptions in Form RM1115, whose paragraph C. directs that asterisked amounts be applied separately and in addition; which rule governs a multi-deductible loss is left to be argued.

The provision is a fragment beginning "below." and turns coverage off at any location for which "a specific value" was not provided, without saying what a specific value is or when it must be provided. The reach of that condition is genuinely uncertain.

This location-by-location value condition is hard to square with the blanket limits shown on the Schedule and with the Errors and Omissions extension (Form RM1002 B.2), which pays where a loss is unpayable solely because of an error in describing or including a location.

"Necessary expenses you incur in excess of your normal operating expenses that reduces your loss of business income" is grammatically broken and overlaps the separate Extra Expense coverage, leaving its boundary unclear.

This clause caps civil-authority business income at twenty-one days, but the LOSS OF BUSINESS INCOME — CIVIL OR MILITARY AUTHORITY AMENDATORY (Form RM1525) deletes and replaces it with a thirty-day, $1,000,000 version. As printed the policy contains two inconsistent versions of C.3.
This twenty-one-day ingress/egress limit is deleted and replaced by Form RM1526, which substitutes thirty days and a $1,000,000 limit, so the policy carries two inconsistent versions of C.4.
"Wholly or partially prevented from producing goods" sets no threshold for what counts as partial prevention, and could be read to require any measurable interference or a substantial one.
The mitigation list is printed with orphaned sub-letters ("d. e.") ahead of the items, and the catch-all "or any other means" leaves the insured's mitigation duty without a stated boundary.

The exclusion of "any consequential, indirect or remote loss" sits inside a coverage that is itself a consequential time-element loss, and the enumerated list is prefaced by broken lettering ("a. e."). Its reach against the grant in C.1 is genuinely contestable.

This twenty-one-day extra-expense civil-authority provision is deleted and replaced by Form RM1523, which substitutes thirty days and a $1,000,000 limit, so two inconsistent versions of D.2 appear in the policy.

The catch-all "any loss or expense recoverable elsewhere in this policy" is set against specific enumerated exclusions, and could be read to strip extra-expense coverage wherever any other extension arguably touches the loss.

The clause pays flood dry-out costs for electrical objects while GROUP A exclusion 3 excludes flood outright and the FLOOD COVERAGE endorsement (Form RM1108) sets its own limits and deductibles; it also cross-refers to G.2. of the Declarations, which contains a checkbox rather than a deductible amount.

The $100,000 accounts receivable limit stated here is increased to $1,000,000 by the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY (Form RM1119) item 1, so the policy carries two different figures for the same sublimit.

"Any loss that requires an audit or inventory to establish its existence" is undefined and could exclude nearly every accounts-receivable claim, since proof of receivables almost always involves accounting records.
"All reasonable efforts, including legal action if necessary" gives no benchmark for how much collection effort is required before the insured may claim.
Payment is the average monthly balance "adjusted for normal fluctuations ... or for any demonstrated variance," terms that supply no measurable standard for the adjustment.

"Fires of a suspicious nature" is a vague trigger, and the reward conditions are drafted so that payment depends on a third party's conviction or confession rather than on anything the insured controls.

The clause promises to pay "up to $25,000" but is written in exclusionary form ("caused by or resulting directly or indirectly from ... regardless of any other cause"), so whether it grants or restricts coverage is genuinely unclear.
"Immediate written notice" is a condition of payment with no defined period, leaving the point at which notice becomes untimely open to argument.
The $250,000 debris removal sublimit stated here is increased to $1,000,000 by the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY (Form RM1119) item 4.A, so two figures appear for the same sublimit.

This $25,000 windblown-debris figure is deleted and replaced by $50,000 in the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY (Form RM1119) item 4.B, so the policy states the same sublimit twice at different amounts.
"All reasonable effort, including legal action against your client" states no measure of what effort suffices before the insurer must pay.

The duty to defend is limited to "that part of any suit" meeting four conditions, yet the insurer reserves the right to settle "as we deem appropriate"; the interaction of a partial defense duty with unilateral settlement discretion is open to competing readings.
The sixty-day extended period stated here is amended to ninety days by the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY (Form RM1119) item 7, so the policy states two different periods.

The breakage exclusion runs to "art glass windows, statuary, marble, glassware, bric-a-brac, porcelains, and similar fragile articles," and the reach of that general catch-all beyond the enumerated items is uncertain.

This extension pays fungus cleanup "up to the applicable limit of liability" while GROUP A exclusion 4 excludes fungus outright except where a specified peril ensues; which controls a fungus claim following fire is left to be harmonised.

The STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY (Form RM1119) item 10 recites that this $250,000 sublimit is "increased ... to $Not Applicable," leaving the operative figure contestable even though the item's box is unchecked.
"Immediate written notice" is an undefined condition precedent, with no stated period against which timeliness can be measured.
The promise to pay pollutant removal "subject to the applicable limit of liability" identifies no sublimit at all, in contrast with the express $25,000 aggregates in the two following subparagraphs.
This $25,000 annual aggregate is increased to $50,000 by the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY (Form RM1119) item 15.A, so the policy states the same aggregate twice at different amounts.
This $25,000 annual aggregate is increased to $50,000 by the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY (Form RM1119) item 15.B, leaving two different figures for the same coverage.
"Immediate written notice" fixes no period, so whether a given delay forfeits the pollution-cleanup expense is left open.
The $25,000 professional-fees sublimit here is increased to $50,000 by the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY (Form RM1119) item 16, so two figures appear for the same sublimit.
Coverage turns on property being at a location "under imminent threat by a peril insured against," a phrase with no temporal or probabilistic boundary.

The ninety-day temporary-location period stated here is deleted and replaced by "up to NA days" in the STANDARD EXTENSIONS AMENDATORY (Form RM1119) item 17, so the operative period is contradicted elsewhere.

The extension applies only where a loss is unpayable "solely because of" an error, then withdraws itself "if coverage is found, in whole or in part, elsewhere in this policy" — a self-cancelling pair of conditions whose combined effect is genuinely obscure.

It is difficult to reconcile with the Declarations Schedule condition that "insurance does not apply at locations ... unless a specific value is provided by you," which appears to defeat the very errors this extension is meant to cure.
This extension pays demolition cost while GROUP A exclusion 6 excludes "demolition cost, operation of building laws and increased cost of construction" without any stated exception for the extension.

The increased construction cost promised here is excluded outright by GROUP A exclusion 6 and is also carved out of the definition of "replacement cost," which excludes increased cost by reason of any law or ordinance.
Payment for rebuilding undamaged parts required by law sits against GROUP A exclusion 6, which excludes operation of building laws generally.
This says unscheduled locations "are insured," but the Declarations item E.4.k shows "$No Coverage" for unscheduled locations and E.1 provides that if no sublimit is shown no coverage is provided.

The anti-concurrent-causation preamble excludes loss "regardless of any other cause or event, including a peril insured against, that contributes to the loss," language whose effect on a mixed-cause loss is a recurring subject of construction.

The exclusion bars earth movement "whether sudden or gradual," while the EARTH MOVEMENT COVERAGE endorsement (Form RM1106) buys back sudden earth movement at scheduled locations; the two must be read together to know what is excluded.
The flat flood exclusion is contradicted in part by the FLOOD COVERAGE endorsement (Form RM1108), which insures flood at scheduled locations with its own limits and deductibles.

The fungus exclusion, with an ensuing-specified-peril exception, must be squared with the Fungus Cleanup Expense extension (Form RM1002 A.10), which pays fungus cleanup following a covered fire or lightning loss.

"Pollution" as defined reaches the presence of any "irritant or contaminant," so the one-word exclusion is capable of swallowing ordinary property damage such as smoke or dust; its intended boundary is genuinely disputable.
The blanket exclusion sits against the Pollution Cleanup Expense extension (Form RM1002 A.15), which pays to remove pollutants following specified and other insured perils.

This exclusion of demolition cost, operation of building laws and increased construction cost directly contradicts the Demolition Cost, Increased Construction Cost and Operation of Building Laws extension (Form RM1002 B.6), for which a $1,000,000 sublimit is shown on the Declarations, and contains no exception for it.
The exclusion lists specific utilities and then adds "or any other service," leaving the catch-all's reach against the enumerated specifics uncertain.
It is qualified by the INTERRUPTION OF SERVICES COVERAGE EXTENSION (Form RM1110), which insures the very off-premises service failures this paragraph excludes.
The exclusion repeatedly closes with "any other electronic equipment, computerized equipment, or similar device," a catch-all whose reach beyond the enumerated computer items is unsettled.
"Unexplained or mysterious disappearance" is not defined and its line against covered theft depends entirely on how much explanation a loss has.

The clause breaks off mid-sentence ("voluntarily relinquishes possession of covered property with or without your"), so the condition on which the exclusion turns is missing; the exclusion of "any criminal, fraudulent or dishonest acts" by "you" or your agents is also broad enough to be read against much ordinary conduct.

An exclusion for "delay, loss of market, loss of use, indirect or remote loss" cannot easily be reconciled with the Loss of Business Income and Extra Expense coverages in Form RM1001 C. and D., which insure precisely that kind of consequential loss.

The exclusion of "wear and tear, deterioration ... inherent vice, latent defect" and of "settling, cracking, shrinking, bulging" of roofs and walls, followed by an ensuing-loss exception, is the classic battleground over whether storm damage to aging building components is excluded deterioration or a covered loss.

The exclusion of machinery failure or breakdown is disapplied by Form RM1001 E.1 wherever the loss results from an "accident" to a covered "object," so its residual scope depends on those definitions.

The exclusion for "faulty, defective or inadequate" construction, workmanship, maintenance or design, coupled with the ensuing-loss exception, requires a line to be drawn between the excluded defect and the covered resulting damage.

The vehicle item both declares highway vehicles beyond 1,000 feet "not covered" and then treats other insurance as "your primary coverage," language that implies this policy does respond in excess; the two halves of the same item point in different directions.

The default replacement-cost valuation is qualified by A.2 (no replacement cost until repair, actual cash value after two years) and by the Vacancy condition, so the operative measure of loss depends on reconciling several provisions.

The clause withholds replacement cost "until the lost or damaged property is actually repaired or replaced" and cuts it off after two years, without saying how that interacts with an insured whose claim is denied and who cannot fund repairs. The trigger and the running of the two years are both open to argument.

It is in tension with the Declarations statement that "this policy provides coverage on a replacement cost basis" and with VALUATIONS A.3, which lets an insured who elects not to rebuild still claim replacement cost.
"Failure to use reasonable speed to repair, rebuild or replace" supplies no timetable, so the amount of any deduction for delay is left at large.
This permits a replacement-cost claim where the insured does not rebuild, which sits awkwardly with A.2's rule that replacement cost is not paid until the property is actually repaired or replaced.
"The proper proportion of overhead charges" gives no method of allocation and is inherently contestable.
"The value blank" is an undefined term of art for valuing damaged records, and its meaning where no blank equivalent exists is unclear.

This makes appraisal available on the unilateral demand of "either party," whereas the KANSAS CHANGES endorsement (Form RM1815) deletes and replaces it with a clause under which "an appraisal will be made only if both parties agree, voluntarily," and extends the appraiser-naming period from thirty to sixty days. Whether appraisal can be compelled turns on which text governs.

Paragraph 2 survives the KANSAS CHANGES endorsement, which replaces only paragraphs 1 and 3, leaving a court-appointed-umpire mechanism attached to an appraisal that under the Kansas text happens only by mutual consent.

This paragraph is deleted and replaced by the KANSAS CHANGES endorsement (Form RM1815) B.3, whose replacement text appears in mutilated form; which version fixes the binding effect of an award is contestable.

The rule that a breach at one location does not affect other locations is hard to reconcile with Condition I, which makes "this entire policy" void for concealment or fraud, and with the Vacancy condition's location-specific sanctions.

This sixty-day threshold for cancellation "for any reason" is deleted and replaced by ninety days in the KANSAS CHANGES — CANCELLATION endorsement (Form RM1915), so the policy states two different periods.

This paragraph and its list of cancellation grounds are deleted and replaced by the KANSAS CHANGES — CANCELLATION endorsement (Form RM1915), which substitutes a ninety-day threshold and a different list of grounds.
The bar on any change except by written endorsement is in tension with Condition K, Liberalization, under which a broadening state filing automatically alters the terms without any endorsement.
The reduction for amounts "collected from others" overlaps Condition Q, Other Insurance, and Condition X, Subrogation, which allocate third-party recoveries on different terms.
The voiding provision lists three actors and four subjects but its numbering restarts, and it is unclear whether the fraud of "any insured" voids coverage for innocent additional named insureds.

It is deleted and replaced for Kansas property by the KANSAS CHANGES endorsement (Form RM1815) I, which forfeits only loss "caused by or resulting from" the fraudulent act rather than voiding the entire policy.

Automatic broadening by a state filing cannot easily be squared with Condition G, Change of Terms, which says the terms will not be waived, changed or modified except by written endorsement issued by the insurer.

The clause operates by reference to loss payees "shown on the SCHEDULE OF MORTGAGE HOLDERS OR LOSS PAYEES, Form RM1102," a form that does not appear on the POLICY INDEX (Form RM0003) or in the policy, so its subject matter is missing.
The paragraph is printed with stray numbering ("1. 5. 6.") before its single sentence, obscuring what falls within it.
It pays mortgage holders shown on Form RM1102, a schedule not listed on the POLICY INDEX and not attached, leaving the clause without any identified beneficiary.

"No person or organization having custody of your covered property will benefit from this policy" is drafted so broadly that its effect on bailees who are themselves additional named insureds, or on the Duty to Defend extension, is unclear.

The non-reduction rule is carved back for coverages "written with an annual aggregate limit," which requires reading it against the aggregate sublimits in the Pollution Cleanup extension and the Earth Movement and Flood endorsements to know what survives a loss.

The pure excess rule in Q.1 sits against Q.2, which contemplates proportionate contribution, and against Q.3-Q.4, which permit other insurance without reduction; how a concurrently insured loss is shared is not settled by any one of them.

The statement that other insurance "will not reduce any limit or sublimit" is difficult to square with Q.1, under which the existence of other insurance postpones this policy's obligation entirely until that insurance is exhausted.

The insurer's option to repair or replace must be exercised "within a reasonable period of time" and notified within sixty days of proof of loss, and the consequence of missing either period is not stated.
The two measures of a pair-or-set loss are joined by "or" with no indication of who chooses or which governs when they differ.
The payment obligation is conditioned on a list reading "1. ...; 2. ..., or 3. ...", so it is unclear whether all three conditions must be met or only the first plus one of the others.

The requirement that loss occur "during the policy period" must be read with the definition of period of restoration, which says expiration does not terminate it, and with the Transit definition, which continues coverage after expiry or cancellation.

The allocation sentence — recovery "in the proportion that your deductible and any provable uninsured loss bears to the total loss less your proportion of fees and expenses" — is syntactically tangled and yields no single arithmetic result.

"Within two (2) years ... or the shortest time permitted by law, whichever is greater" is internally confused: pairing the *shortest* period permitted by law with a "whichever is greater" test makes the applicable limitation period genuinely uncertain.

The KANSAS CHANGES endorsement (Form RM1815) deletes and replaces this condition with a five-year period running from the date the physical damage occurred, so the policy contains two different suit limitations.
"A dangerous condition relating to an object" permits immediate unilateral suspension of coverage without any defined standard for what is dangerous.
"Protective safeguards include, but are not limited to" a list of five systems, so the insured cannot tell what else it must maintain in complete working order to preserve coverage.

The second sanction ("Value the loss or damage ...") appears without its sub-letter, so it is unclear whether the valuation rule is an independent consequence or part of the preceding list of non-covered perils.
"Immediate written notice of the loss" fixes no period and is a condition on which several extensions expressly depend; what delay forfeits coverage is left entirely to argument.
The duties are printed with orphaned sub-letters ("a. b.") ahead of three separate obligations, and "as often as may reasonably be required" supplies no limit on repeated examinations under oath.

The ninety-day sworn proof of loss requirement interacts with Condition T, which makes payment due thirty days after an accepted proof, and with the suit limitation; whether a late proof forfeits the claim is not addressed.
"A sudden, fortuitous event" is undefined, and the carve-outs for "any other gradually developing condition" and conditions correctable by maintenance leave the boundary of an "accident" open.
"Replacement cost less deduction for depreciation" does not say whether depreciation may be taken on labour as well as materials, a recurring point of dispute.
"Less all charges and expenses which do not necessarily continue" is the operative deduction and turns on a judgment about necessity that the definition does not further specify.

The definition limits covered locations to those "shown on the Schedule," but the Declarations Schedule itself identifies covered locations only as those "per Statement of Values on file with us," a document outside the policy; which controls whether a given building is insured is genuinely contestable.
The definition is circular: a "covered loss" requires a "peril insured against," which is itself defined as a cause of loss "for which this policy provides coverage."

It confines covered loss to property "at a covered location," while Form RM1001 A. and B. insure property within 1,000 feet of a covered location and several extensions insure property in transit or away from any covered location.
"Covered property means property insured by this policy" is wholly circular and does no defining work, yet the term is the trigger for the insuring agreement and most exclusions.
"Earth movement ... includes but is not limited to" four enumerated events, so the reach of the definition beyond earthquake, landslide, mudflow and sinking of earth is left open.
"Reasonable and necessary extra costs" to continue business "as nearly normal as practicable" supplies no measurable ceiling on what qualifies.
"Property of rarity, antiquity, or artistic merit, including but not limited to" a long list leaves the general standard undefined and the catch-all's reach uncertain.

"Flood" is defined to include "surface water, rain accumulation or runoff ... whether driven by wind or not," which is broad enough to capture ordinary rain entry and collides with the ordinary understanding of flood.

Hail is defined as stones "ranging in size from pea to softball or larger," a formulation that on its face excludes hail smaller than a pea and gives no guidance on measurement; the definition governs whether a hail claim is a covered specified peril at all.

"Miscellaneous location" is defined only negatively, including by reference to any location "for which coverage is found, in whole or in part, elsewhere in this policy," which makes the category self-referential.

"Principally used ... away from a covered location" gives no test for how much off-site use is enough, and the definition simultaneously includes machinery attached to a highway vehicle while excluding the vehicle itself.

The Named Storm 72-hour aggregation sits against the general "occurrence" definition, which aggregates similar causes "irrespective of the amount of time," and the named-storm deductible in Form RM1115 is keyed only to first and second tier counties, none of which are in Kansas.

"Equipment ... that generates, transmits or utilizes energy" is broad enough to take in almost any powered item, and is then cut back by a thirteen-item exclusion list; where the line falls is genuinely arguable.

"All loss or damage attributable directly or indirectly to one cause or series of similar causes ... irrespective of the amount of time or area" leaves it open whether successive storms months apart are one occurrence or many, which drives both the limit and the deductible.

It cannot be readily harmonised with the 72-hour aggregation clocks in the Named Storm definition and the Earth Movement and Flood endorsements, or the 168-hour clock for volcanic activity, all of which assume time does limit an occurrence.
"Perils insured against means causes of loss for which this policy provides coverage" defines the term by reference to the very coverage it is used to establish, and is therefore circular.

The period ends when the property "using reasonable speed" could be repaired and made ready for operations, a hypothetical measure with no fixed benchmark; the paragraph is also printed with missing sub-letters and numbering.

The three limbs of the definition run together without their numbering, so it is unclear whether property must satisfy one or all of them, and the final limb is capped by "your insurable interest" while the first two are not.
"Policy period means the time during which insurance is provided by this policy" is circular and adds nothing to the dates shown on the Declarations.

"Any solid, liquid, gaseous or thermal irritant or contaminant, including, but not limited to" a long list, with an express carve-out only for ammonia, is a general catch-all against enumerated specifics whose reach over ordinary building materials is much litigated.

"Machinery and equipment used to service the buildings" is included in real property while the personal property definition sweeps in all "tangible things, other than real property," so items such as HVAC units may fall under either heading and different limits.

Replacement cost is defined to exclude increased cost imposed by law or ordinance, while the Demolition Cost, Increased Construction Cost and Operation of Building Laws extension pays that very cost under a $1,000,000 sublimit.
The list of specified perils ends with "Collapse," a term left undefined anywhere in the policy even though it triggers the fungus and pollution provisions.

The definition presupposes coverage for unscheduled locations, but the Declarations item E.4.k shows "$No Coverage" for unscheduled locations and E.1 states that where no sublimit is shown no coverage is provided.

"Wind means the direct action of the movement of air at any velocity" is so broad that any air movement qualifies, which matters for the named-storm deductible and for separating wind damage from excluded causes.

Confining "you" to "the named insured shown on the DECLARATIONS" is hard to square with the ADDITIONAL NAMED INSURED endorsement (Form RM1100), which extends insurance to seven further entities while every coverage grant is expressed in terms of "your" property.

Extending insurance to additional named insureds is difficult to reconcile with the definition of "you and your(s)" as the named insured on the Declarations, since the coverage forms insure only "your real property" and "your personal property".

Adjusting "only with you" sits against Condition W.2, which gives the insurer the right to adjust directly with owners of property of others, and against the endorsement's own requirement of joint payment to the additional named insureds.

Mandatory joint payment to every scheduled additional named insured is awkward beside the immediately preceding sentence that loss is adjusted "only with you," and beside Condition L's loss payee machinery.

The $25,000 per-item caps must be read with the schedule's $1,000,000 limit and with PROPERTY NOT COVERED item J., which excludes mobile equipment more than 1,000 feet from a covered location; the endorsement modifies but does not expressly delete that exclusion.
The buy-back covers only "sudden" earth movement, a qualifier the policy never defines, and the underlying exclusion applies to earth movement "whether sudden or gradual."
The carve-out is keyed to Form RM1105 (Earth Movement Sprinkler Leakage Extension), which is not listed on the POLICY INDEX and is not part of this policy, leaving the sentence without a referent.
The 72-hour single-occurrence rule conflicts in principle with the general definition of "occurrence," which aggregates similar causes irrespective of the amount of time over which loss occurs.

The percentage-deductible machinery is triggered only "if a percentage deductible is shown on the Schedule," but the endorsement's own Schedule shows only flat $50,000 amounts, leaving the paragraph with nothing to operate on.
The list withholds earth movement coverage from Form RM1112, a Contingent Loss of Business Income extension that is not listed on the POLICY INDEX and forms no part of this policy.
The list of excluded states is printed with corrupted lettering ("Af = op aw >") between the marked items, so which sub-paragraph each (X) belongs to cannot be read off the text.
The grant of flood coverage must be read against GROUP A exclusion 3, which excludes flood outright, and against the Schedule, which limits the buy-back to identified locations.

Treating all flood losses in a rolling 72-hour window as one occurrence is at odds with the general "occurrence" definition, which aggregates similar causes irrespective of the time over which loss occurs.
The exclusion list refers to Form RM1112, which is not on the POLICY INDEX and is not part of this policy.

The covered off-premises property is described as listed plants and then "any other plant or facility responsible for providing the services specified," a catch-all whose reach against the enumerated specifics is uncertain, and the alternative "located within one (1) mile" test is undefined as to measurement.

The deductible is imported from G.3.a and G.3.b of the Declarations, where every equipment-breakdown figure reads "$Not Applicable" except a cross-reference back to Form RM1115, producing a circular deductible reference.
The time deductible is expressed as "a time period of Not Applicable," which is not a period at all, yet the sentence that follows explains how days are counted.
The asterisk rule makes marked deductibles cumulative, which pulls against the Declarations G. rule and Form RM1115 B. that no more than the largest applicable deductible will be used.

The four excepted categories are joined by "and" rather than "or," so it is unclear whether an employee must fall into all of them to be excluded, and the sentence then runs straight on to "and Payroll expense includes," mixing exclusion and inclusion in one broken sentence.

The "largest deductible only" rule is immediately qualified by paragraph C., which makes asterisked amounts cumulative, and by the named-storm provision, which adds factors together; the three rules must be reconciled to compute any deductible.

The instruction to add all applicable percentage and flat factors together conflicts with paragraph B. of the same endorsement and with Declarations G., which say no more than the largest applicable deductible will be used.

Only first and second tier wind counties are listed as categories, and the tie-break rule ("the category that more specifically identifies that location") gives no criterion of specificity; for a Kansas location no category applies at all.

The named-storm deductible is keyed to the First and Second tier wind Counties definitions, none of which include any Kansas county, so it cannot operate on the only locations scheduled under this policy.
The heading is mutilated ("e€ or Rented Mobile Equipment or Tools"), leaving the category to which the $5,000 deductible attaches to be inferred.

The waiting period is stated as "Not Applicable hours," so the condition cannot be applied as written even though the next sentence tells the reader what happens "once the waiting period has been exceeded."
This raises the Accounts Receivable sublimit to $1,000,000 while Form RM1002 A.1.a still reads $100,000, so the policy states the same sublimit at two amounts.
The item purports to increase the Arson Reward sublimit "from $25,000 to $Not Applicable," which states no amount; with the selection box unchecked it is unclear whether anything is changed.
The item recites an increase "from $25,000 to $Not Applicable," a figure that cannot be applied; whether the unchecked box leaves the original sublimit intact is left to inference.
This raises the debris removal sublimit to $1,000,000 while Form RM1002 A.4.b still reads $250,000, leaving two figures in the instrument.
This replacement sets windblown-debris removal at $50,000 while the unamended text of Form RM1002 A.4.c still reads $25,000.
The item recites an increase "from $25,000 to $Not Applicable," which is not a limit; the unchecked box leaves its operative effect uncertain.
This amends the extended period of restoration to ninety days while Form RM1002 A.7.a still states sixty days, so the policy contains both periods.
The item is printed without its selection box and recites an increase "to $Not Applicable," so neither whether it applies nor what amount it sets can be read from the text.
The item lost its selection marker and recites an increase "from $250,000 to $Not Applicable," leaving both its applicability and its amount indeterminate.
The item lost its selection marker and recites an increase "from $250,000 to $Not Applicable," which states no operative sublimit.
The item recites an increase "from $25,000 to $Not Applicable" without any selection marker, so its effect on the lock and key sublimit cannot be determined from the words.
The item recites an increase "from $100,000 to $Not Applicable" without a selection marker, leaving the operative sublimit for plants, trees or shrubs unstated.
This sets the pollution cleanup aggregate at $50,000 while Form RM1002 A.15.b still reads $25,000.
This sets the land and water pollution cleanup aggregate at $50,000 while Form RM1002 A.15.c still reads $25,000.
This raises professional fees to $50,000 while Form RM1002 A.16.a still reads $25,000, so two figures stand in the policy.
The replacement text reads "For up to NA days at each place to which the property has been taken," which states no period and cannot be applied as a coverage term.
It purports to delete and replace the ninety-day temporary-location period in Form RM1002 A.17.b(1), so the policy contains two irreconcilable statements of how long removed property stays insured.

The extension grants penalty coverage by "modifying" Form RM1001 C.8.b(2), which excludes fines or damages "for penalties of any nature," and the same exclusion is repeated in the Extra Expense exclusions at D.3.e(2), which the endorsement does not touch.

Payment requires that the insured "be found to be legally liable" for the penalties, without saying by whom or in what forum, while paragraph 3 disclaims any duty to defend the very proceeding that would produce such a finding.

"The policy deductible" is not a single figure: Declarations G. states $10,000 but marks the box directing the reader to Form RM1115, which lists several category deductibles and none for contract penalties.
The definition says the TRIA criteria "include the following" and then lists two, so the list is non-exhaustive and the boundary of a certified act as used in the exclusion is left open.

The fire buy-back gives the full limit only in the states on the endorsement's Schedule, which does not include Kansas, so every scheduled location in this policy falls under the $1,000,000 alternative — a result at odds with the $65,808,311 blanket limit on the Declarations.

"The reasonable extra costs of temporary repair to property or of expediting the permanent repair ... whichever is less" leaves it unclear whether the comparison is between the two categories of cost or between cost and some other measure.

The clause redefines "extra expenses" locally for hazardous substance cleanup, while "extra expense" is a defined policy term in Form RM1007 L. carrying a different meaning; which meaning governs is left to be worked out.

Payment is to be determined "in accordance with the valuations endorsement," but the policy contains a VALUATIONS form (RM1005) and no valuations endorsement, so the cross-reference has no clear referent.

This promises up to $100,000 for the cost to "research, replace and restore lost data," whereas VALUATIONS C.4 states that the insurer will not pay any cost "including research ... of restoring or recreating lost information."
"Any substance that is hazardous to health" has no boundary at all apart from the alternative of a governmental declaration, so almost any contaminant could qualify.
This replacement gives thirty days and a $1,000,000 limit, while the unamended text of Form RM1001 D.2 still appears in the policy with a twenty-one day period and no separate limit.
This replacement gives thirty days and a $1,000,000 limit, while Form RM1001 C.3 as printed still states twenty-one days, so the policy carries both versions.
This replacement gives thirty days and a $1,000,000 limit for ingress/egress business income, while Form RM1001 C.4 as printed still states twenty-one days.

Limiting the Kansas amendments to "covered property located in Kansas" leaves the time-element coverages, which are not property located anywhere, arguably outside the endorsement even though every scheduled location is in Wichita.

The paragraph first says "either party may require that the amount be submitted for appraisal" and then says "an appraisal will be made only if both parties agree, voluntarily," two sentences that cannot both be given their natural effect.

It deletes and replaces Condition B.1 of Form RM1006, which allows either party to compel appraisal on written demand within sixty days, so whether appraisal is mandatory or consensual depends on which text controls.

The text is mutilated and breaks off mid-sentence ("Wee agreement —_ by any two (2) of these three (3) ... An appraisa p i"), so the rule on the binding effect of an appraisal award cannot be read from the provision.
It deletes and replaces Condition B.3 of Form RM1006, whose intact text makes the two-of-three written agreement conclusive as to the amount of loss.
This replaces Condition I of Form RM1006, which voids the entire policy for fraud; the two provisions attach very different consequences to the same conduct and both appear in the instrument.
The act must consist of "written statements where the known intent is to defraud," a formulation that leaves whose knowledge and intent count, and whether oral misstatements are caught, unresolved.

This five-year suit limitation replaces Condition Y of Form RM1006, which as printed requires suit within two years "or the shortest time permitted by law, whichever is greater"; the policy therefore states two limitation periods.
This ninety-day threshold replaces the sixty-day threshold in Condition F.2 of Form RM1006, which remains printed in the policy.
This substitutes a different list of cancellation grounds and notice periods for Condition F.3 of Form RM1006, which remains printed with its own, differing list.

The notice speaks of coverage "made available" and premium "shown on the DECLARATIONS," where the terrorism premium entry reads "$Declined"; read with the EXCLUSION OF CERTIFIED ACT(S) OF TERRORISM endorsement, whether any terrorism coverage exists must be inferred rather than read.

This states the cap by reference to a "calendar year" while the EXCLUSION OF CERTIFIED ACT(S) OF TERRORISM endorsement paragraph 4 states the same cap by reference to a "program year (January 1 through December 31)".
